title: Amba, born again
hook: the warrior Bhishma won't fight carries a grievance from a whole lifetime before the war: the princess Amba
carry: karma can follow you into another birth
tomorrow: two kinds of arrows hit Bhishma. can he tell them apart?

segments.voice: Yesterday the Pandavas crossed the dark field, and Bhishma kept to satya, telling them the truth that would end him. Your line: satya: truth is dharma, even against yourself.
screen: `THE TRUTH THAT WOULD END HIM.` · `SATYA: TRUTH IS DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Why Shikhandi? Bhishma has held off whole armies without flinching. Why would one warrior from Drupada's house make him lower his bow? The epic's answer starts long before this war, before the Pandavas were born, at a bride-choosing in the kingdom of Kashi. Bhishma arrives there, not for himself, but for his younger half-brother, who needs a wife. He carries off the princesses of Kashi in his chariot. One of those princesses is named Amba. Today, her story.
screen: `WHY SHIKHANDI?` → `A BRIDE-CHOOSING IN KASHI.` → `A PRINCESS NAMED AMBA.`

segments.voice: Back in Hastinapura, Amba says her heart was already given to King Shalva. Bhishma lets her go to him. But Shalva won't take her back: another man carried you off, he says in effect, go to him. And Bhishma won't take her either. Long ago he swore never to marry, the vow that, the text says, earned him the name Bhishma, the one of the terrible vow. Every door is shut, and in Amba's eyes one man shut them all. Even Parashurama, Bhishma's own teacher, fights him for her and can't win. So Amba turns to austerity, and Shiva grants her wish: in another birth she will be the cause of Bhishma's death. She enters the fire, and is born again in King Drupada's house as a daughter, raised as a son, who later becomes a man, Shikhandi. And Bhishma knows all of it. When he lowers his bow before Shikhandi, he's looking at Amba. Here's the teaching under the story. Hindus believe in karma and rebirth: what we do bears fruit, and the self, the atman, isn't finished when one body ends. The Gita puts it simply: as a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves one body and takes another. A wrong done in one life doesn't vanish. And notice who did it: not a villain, but a man keeping a promise to his father and winning brides for his brother. Good intentions don't cancel karma.
screen: `EVERY DOOR SHUT` · `SHIVA'S PROMISE` · `BORN AGAIN AS SHIKHANDI` · then, large: `KARMA ACROSS BIRTHS`

segments.voice: Hindus have an old way of carrying karma: offering what you do to God. In the Gita, Krishna says whatever you do, whatever you eat or give, make it an offering to me, and many families end a puja with the words Krishnarpanam astu: may this be offered to Krishna. Bring to mind one choice you made for good reasons that still landed hard on someone. Breathe in and see the person it reached. Breathe out and, if you pray, offer it: Krishnarpanam astu. If you don't, simply wish that person well.
Bhishma's fall. It starts with a princess whose life had no open door, and a promise that she would be the cause of his death.
Your line: karma can follow you into another birth. Behind Shikhandi stands Amba. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Amba's story is told in the Udyoga Parva of the Mahabharata, and retellings of the epic return to it when they reach Bhishma's fall, to explain why he will not fight Shikhandi.
